A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same optimization problem, algorithms and research contributions. Their main text, equations, numerical figures and complete appendices support comparison, including the new Appendix F in v2.

before.justification: Section 7 and Figures 7.1–7.3 report original numerical comparisons of gradient methods on power-function minimization problems.

after.justification: Section 7 and Figures 7.1–7.4 report original numerical results, including expanded normalized-gradient comparisons and a new good-starting-point experiment.

M1.justification: The basic gradient, normalized-gradient, Polyak and AGMsDR updates are retained. The two-stage procedure now also permits the existing clipped rule (3.6), and Section 6 changes its prescribed acceleration constant from 3L0 to 5L0/(2a), with a depending on the stepsize rule.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate minimization of f(x)=||x||^p/p with p=4,6,8. The added initialization and parameter-sensitivity experiments vary settings within this retained function family and optimization task.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same methods: the gradient stepsize variants, normalized gradient, Polyak and AccGD in Figure 7.1, and gradient descent, AccGD, STM and STM-Max in Figure 7.3. Additional normalized-gradient curves vary a parameter. NAG receives theoretical analysis but no empirical comparison.

E3.justification: Figure 7.3 changes initial distances from {5,100,500} to {10,100,1000}, extends the plotted horizon from 2500 to 5000 iterations, and changes the reported acceleration parameter from 4L0 to 3L0. Figure 7.1 expands distance-estimate settings, while Figure 7.4 introduces initialization satisfying F0≤L0/(5L1²), bypassing the first stage.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained smoothness-parameter and initial-distance studies, v2 tests normalized-gradient sensitivity to the estimated initial distance in Figure 7.1. New Figure 7.4 isolates the accelerated stage through good initialization. These additions test two central practical assumptions that v1 did not systematically examine.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests for its deterministic numerical comparisons.

E6.justification: Figure 7.1 adds normalized-gradient curves labeled 0.1-NGD, 0.5-NGD and 10-NGD alongside the retained 2R setting. Figure 7.4 adds the finding that STM and STM-Max outperform AccGD for p=6,8 under good initialization, while the accelerated methods are reported as comparable for p=4. Figure 7.3 also replaces convergence curves under revised settings, rather than establishing a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.2 introduces the finer O(L0R²/ε+L1R ln(F0/ε)) bound with a new distance-monotonicity lemma and integral proof. Appendix A.6 supplies previously absent supporting proofs, Appendix C develops the existing decreasing-stepsize discussion into an explicit complexity theorem, and new Appendix F derives a rescaled-NAG bound. Several convergence constants and iteration-count formulas are also revised.

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion replace the convex-GM headline bound O(L0R²/ε+L1²R²) with O(L0R²/ε+L1R ln(F0/ε)); normalized-gradient and Polyak guarantees retain the former order. The acceleration headline now explicitly includes the line-search oracle factor m, which v1 discussed only in the detailed analysis.

C2.justification: V2 explains when bounded initial residuals make the finer GM bound advantageous and describes normalized gradient's guarantee as generally worse than that bound. It explicitly acknowledges the need for f* to stop the first acceleration stage, expands the sublevel-set explanation, and qualifies empirical advantages through best-iterate behavior and the new good-initialization results.

D1.justification: V2 explains the distinct normalization rules of STM and STM-Max and more explicitly documents acceleration inputs and stopping requirements. However, it removes v1's explicit R=10 specification for Figure 7.1, and its listed distance estimates omit the plotted 0.1R case. Neither version provides code-access or hardware information.

R1.justification: V2 changes its comparison with Gorbunov et al. from matching the convex-GM complexity to obtaining a potentially sharper bound. It replaces the previously quoted NAG rate with the rescaled bound derived in Appendix F, substantially revising the theoretical comparison with Li et al. It also adds Rodomanov's thesis as a supporting reference.

P1.justification: Section 2 moves examples and closure operations before the first-order characterizations. Section 6 substantially rewrites the acceleration explanation and presents AGMsDR before the two-stage procedure. Appendix C is reorganized into general, constant-stepsize and decreasing-stepsize analyses, alongside terminology and prose revisions throughout.

P2.justification: V2 expands Figure 7.1's legend, redraws convergence displays, extends Figure 7.3's iteration axis and adds the three-panel Figure 7.4. Figures and algorithm boxes are rearranged, while the overall document and plotting styles remain similar.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's coarser convex bound and brief decreasing-stepsize analysis, v2 supplies a finer Theorem 3.2 with a new proof and a detailed Theorem C.2. Appendix F makes the NAG comparison inspectable, while explicit oracle costs, stopping requirements and good-initialization results better qualify the acceleration contribution. These substantially strengthen this theory-centered paper despite minor experimental reporting inconsistencies.
